inline_comments.comment: All five top-level imports — `readFileSync`, `writeFileSync` (node:fs), `find` (empathic/find), `detectIndent` (detect-indent), `join` (pathe), and `getProjectRoot` (./utils/paths.ts) — are imported but never referenced by any of the three exported functions (`formatMinVersion`, `isNodeVersionSupported`, `parseNodeVersionString`). The file is 133 lines total (confirmed) and contains no other code. These dead imports add unnecessary transitive dependencies to every consumer of `storybook/internal/common`, and mean that a failure to resolve `empathic/find` or `detect-indent` would break the Node version check at startup for no reason. Remove them, or add the file-I/O helper functions (e.g., for reading/updating `.nvmrc`) that the PR description claims exist here.

`join` from `pathe` is imported but unused (see the broader unused-imports comment on line 1). Worth calling out separately because `pathe` is a transitive dep of `node-version.ts` — removing the unused imports means consumers don't pay for it.

The three `vi.mock` calls at the top of the test file (`empathic/find`, `node:fs`, `./utils/paths.ts`) are needed only because the production module unconditionally imports those modules at the top level — not because any tested function actually calls into them. If the unused imports are removed from `node-version.ts` (as flagged), these mocks become unnecessary and should be deleted. As written, they give a misleading impression that the tested functions exercise filesystem or path logic.

`export {}` is a non-obvious incantation. Add a short inline comment explaining why it's here — e.g., `// Needed to enable top-level await in this ESM entry-point script`. Without the comment, a future reader will waste time figuring out why a bare export statement exists in a CLI entry point.

`storybook/internal/common` is imported twice: once on line 4 for `isNodeVersionSupported`, then again here for `MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_DESCRIPTION`. Node.js caches the module so there is no double-evaluation, but the split creates visual noise and could confuse readers. Since `MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_DESCRIPTION` is a string constant, pulling it out in the first import (`const { isNodeVersionSupported, MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_DESCRIPTION } = await import(...)`) has negligible startup cost and makes the error path simpler.

The error message no longer includes "Please upgrade your Node.js installation." This guidance was present in the original code and is still present in both `code/core/src/bin/dispatcher.ts` and `code/lib/cli-storybook/src/bin/index.ts`. The omission is a regression: a user who hits this path from `create-storybook` receives no actionable next step, while users of the other entry points do. Add the sentence back for consistency.

`logger.outro('')` is called with an empty string immediately before `process.exit(1)`. An empty `outro` renders a blank closing-box UI element, which looks odd paired with an error message. Neither `dispatcher.ts` nor `cli-storybook/src/bin/index.ts` calls `outro` in the equivalent error path. Either omit this call or pass a meaningful closing string (e.g., `'Exiting.'`) so the output is intentional rather than accidental.

general_comments.comment: The new `isNodeVersionSupported` changes the runtime behavior for Node.js versions whose major falls between the two defined supported ranges — most notably Node.js 21.x. The old inline checks only rejected versions below 20, or 20.x with minor < 19, or 22.x with minor < 12; Node.js 21.x passed through as 'supported'. The new function explicitly rejects any major not in `MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_VERSIONS` unless it exceeds `maxDefinedMajor`. This is arguably more correct (21 is EOL), but it is an undocumented behavioral change that could break CI pipelines or developer machines still on 21.x. The change should be called out explicitly in the PR description, and the `dispatcher.ts` / `cli-storybook` error message could mention that supported majors are 20 and 22 (not just a version number floor).

The `MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_DESCRIPTION` constant test (`expect(MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_DESCRIPTION).toBe('20.19+ or 22.12+')`) hard-codes the human-readable string. When `MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_VERSIONS` is next updated, this test will fail with a raw string mismatch rather than a clear 'you forgot to update the description' message. Consider asserting the computed value instead — e.g., `expect(MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_DESCRIPTION).toBe(MIN_SUPPORTED_NODE_VERSIONS.map(formatMinVersion).join(' or '))` — so the test catches missing coverage rather than just the current string value.
